reading.body:
CyrusOne Sterling (NVA4) in northern Virginia publishes 11 MW of IT load capacity, which at typical AI training density translates to roughly 275 racks or approximately 2,200 accelerators, a modest single-facility footprint insufficient to anchor large-scale model training.

Sterling ranks 22nd among Virginia's 25 facilities with published capacity figures, holding 0.7% of the state's disclosed power. Virginia itself has 330 mapped data center locations but only 25 publish power specifications, meaning the vast majority of the state's infrastructure capacity remains hidden from view. Among those that do report, Sterling is mid-tier by consumption.

The facility spans 128,715 square feet of technical space and lists no certifications, a profile consistent with regional colocation serving enterprise and cloud tenants rather than hyperscale AI training infrastructure. This matters for AI compute scaling because 11 MW cannot run a meaningful training workload; the largest model training clusters operate at hundreds of megawatts or more. Sterling's disclosure provides one data point in Virginia's infrastructure landscape, but obscured capacity at the other 305 undisclosed facilities means the state's true compute density for AI remains unknown.
